title: Connector framework — interface, scheduler, cursor store
description: The Go Connector interface from the architecture doc, plus a scheduler that runs connectors per tenant on an interval and persists cursors transactionally.
acceptance: Adding a new source requires implementing one interface and registering it — no change to ingest, detection or correlation
Cursors are committed to Postgres only after the batch is durably acknowledged by Kafka
The scheduler isolates failures: one failing tenant or connector does not stall others
Per-connector health is exposed as a metric and surfaced through the API
Graceful shutdown drains in-flight batches before exiting

tests.desc: Cursor advances only after a successful Kafka acknowledgement
A connector returning an error does not advance its cursor
One tenant's failing connector does not delay another tenant's schedule
SIGTERM during a batch drains cleanly with no partial commit

title: Microsoft 365 OAuth onboarding and consent flow
description: Admin consent flow for the Microsoft 365 Management Activity API and Graph audit logs, with least-privilege read-only scopes and encrypted credential storage.
acceptance: Only read-only scopes are requested; the requested scope list is documented and justified in the repo
Refresh tokens are envelope-encrypted with a per-tenant DEK
The consent flow completes in under 10 minutes for a non-technical admin
Token refresh is automatic, with clear surfacing when consent is revoked
Revoking the connector deletes stored credentials and stops collection within one scheduling interval

tests.desc: Full consent flow against a Microsoft test tenant yields a working token
Stored credentials are unreadable without the KMS key
Expired access token triggers a transparent refresh
Revoked consent surfaces as a degraded connector health state, not a silent stall

title: M365 Management Activity API collector with blob checkpointing
description: Subscribe to M365 audit content types, enumerate available content blobs, fetch and parse them, and checkpoint by blob id so a restart never re-processes or skips.
acceptance: Subscribes to Audit.Exchange, Audit.SharePoint, Audit.AzureActiveDirectory and Audit.General
Blob ids form the checkpoint; a restart resumes exactly where it stopped
Microsoft throttling (429) is honoured with Retry-After backoff
Blobs that fail to parse go to the DLQ with the raw content preserved, never dropped
Collection keeps pace with a 1,000-seat tenant within one scheduling interval

tests.desc: Recorded API fixtures produce the expected set of raw events
Restart mid-batch resumes without loss or observable duplication
429 with Retry-After is respected rather than hot-retried
Malformed blob routes to DLQ with raw content intact
Sustains a simulated 1,000-seat tenant inside one interval

title: OCSF normalisation for M365 event families
description: Implements ADR-0002 for M365: sign-in, mailbox, file, admin and consent activity mapped to OCSF classes. Pure and total — no I/O, no clock, no network.
acceptance: Normalise is a pure function with no I/O, enforced by review and by the absence of injected clients
Unmapped vendor fields are preserved under unmapped rather than discarded
Every event carries event_id, tenant_id, time and schema_version

event_id is deterministic from the source event and stable across re-normalisation — the grounding validator in P4-04 resolves claims by this id, so an unstable id silently breaks the product's central guarantee
Timestamps are normalised to UTC with the original offset retained
A mapping coverage report lists which M365 operations are mapped and which are not

tests.desc: Golden fixture per event family maps to the expected OCSF output, byte for byte
Unknown event type is preserved rather than dropped or erroring
Property test: normalisation is deterministic across repeated invocations
Timezone handling is correct for events in non-UTC offsets, including DST boundaries
event_id survives ingest to ClickHouse unchanged and is resolvable by a lookup query — the operation the grounding validator performs
Re-normalising the same raw payload after a replay produces the identical event_id, so previously grounded claims stay resolvable

title: Redpanda topics, partitioning and producer
description: Topic creation with the partition counts and retention from the architecture doc, keyed by tenant with a reserved shard suffix, plus a batching idempotent producer.
acceptance: Topics are created declaratively and are idempotent to re-apply
Keys use the tenant_id:shard_n format from day one, with shard 0 as the default
The producer batches and uses idempotent delivery
A DLQ topic exists for every main topic
Per-tenant ordering is preserved and verified

tests.desc: Topic provisioning is idempotent across repeated runs
Events for one tenant arrive in production order on a single partition
Producer retries on broker unavailability without duplicating or reordering

title: ClickHouse event schema, partitioning and TTL
description: Implements ADR-0005. ReplacingMergeTree keyed on (tenant_id, event_id), partitioned by day, ordered tenant-first, with a TTL policy moving cold partitions to object storage.
acceptance: ORDER BY (tenant_id, time, event_id) so every tenant-scoped query uses the primary index
ReplacingMergeTree collapses the duplicates at-least-once ingest produces
Partitioned by day with a 90-day hot TTL and an S3 cold tier
Row policies enforce tenant isolation at the storage layer
A 30-day single-identity lookup over a billion-row table returns in under one second

tests.desc: Duplicate insert of the same event_id collapses after merge
Row policy blocks a cross-tenant read
Benchmark: 30-day identity lookup under one second at one billion rows
TTL moves an aged partition to the cold tier and queries still return it

title: Kafka-to-ClickHouse ingest writer with batching
description: Consumes normalised events and writes them to ClickHouse in batches sized for merge health, with offset commits only after a durable write.
acceptance: Batched inserts only — never per-row
Offsets commit after the ClickHouse write is acknowledged
Backpressure propagates: a slow ClickHouse slows consumption rather than buffering unboundedly
Merge queue depth is monitored and alerted on
Sustains 30,000 events per second in the load test

tests.desc: Consumer restart replays uncommitted offsets with no data loss
ClickHouse unavailability pauses consumption and recovers without loss
Sustains 30k EPS for 15 minutes with stable merge queue depth
Batch sizing respects both the row-count and time-window triggers

title: Raw log archive to object storage
description: Every raw vendor payload is archived before normalisation, partitioned by tenant and date, so a mapping bug is recoverable by replay rather than by apology.
acceptance: Raw payloads are written before normalisation, never after
Partitioned by tenant_id and date for efficient selective replay
Compressed, with lifecycle rules for the retention tier
Server-side encrypted at rest
Archive write failure fails the batch rather than silently proceeding

tests.desc: Every ingested event has a corresponding archived raw payload
Archive write failure causes batch failure, not silent continuation
Lifecycle policy transitions an aged object to the cheaper storage class

title: Replay tooling — re-ingest historical raw events
description: Re-run archived raw events through normalisation and detection for a tenant and time range. This is how mapping bugs are fixed and it is the engine behind the free 7-day security scan.
acceptance: Replay is scoped by tenant and time range and never touches another tenant
Replay is idempotent — re-running produces no observable duplication
Replay can target a separate output topic so production state is not disturbed
Progress is reported and the job is resumable after interruption
Replaying 7 days for a 100-seat tenant completes in under 10 minutes

tests.desc: Replay of a known range reproduces the identical normalised event set
Replay twice produces no duplicate rows after merge
Interrupted replay resumes from its checkpoint
7-day replay for a 100-seat tenant completes inside 10 minutes

title: Per-tenant rate limiting and ingest backpressure
description: Token-bucket quotas in Redis so a tenant emitting 50x its normal volume cannot starve the others. Overflow spills to archive for later replay instead of being dropped.
acceptance: Per-tenant EPS quota is configurable and defaults by plan tier
Exceeding the quota throttles that tenant's fetch rate without affecting others
Overflow is archived for replay, never discarded
Quota breaches are surfaced to the tenant and to operations
Redis unavailability fails open with a conservative global limit rather than halting ingest

tests.desc: A tenant at 50x normal volume does not increase another tenant's ingest lag
Token bucket refills at the configured rate
Redis outage degrades to the global limit and ingest continues

title: Ingest observability — lag, EPS and connector health
description: The metrics needed to answer 'is this tenant's data flowing' without reading logs, plus alerting on ingest lag.
acceptance: Ingest lag is measured per tenant and per connector and exported as a metric
EPS, batch size and error rate are exported per connector
Alert fires when ingest lag exceeds 5 minutes
Connector health is visible through the API for the dashboard to render
A dashboard panel shows the 20 most-lagging tenants

tests.desc: Induced connector stall produces a lag metric increase and fires the alert
Lag calculation is correct when a connector has produced no events at all
Health endpoint reflects a revoked-consent connector as degraded

title: 72-hour continuous ingest soak with induced failures
description: The P1 exit criterion as an executable test: run continuously for 72 hours against a seeded tenant while injecting broker, database and vendor-API failures, and reconcile counts.
acceptance: Runs 72 hours continuously without manual intervention
Injects broker restart, ClickHouse restart, and vendor 429 and 503 responses
Produced count reconciles exactly with stored count after merge
No unhandled panic or goroutine leak over the run
A written report of lag distribution and failure recovery times is produced

tests.desc: Count reconciliation is exact after induced broker restart
Count reconciliation is exact after induced ClickHouse restart
Memory and goroutine counts are stable across the full 72 hours

title: Connector developer guide and the second-connector dry run
description: Prove the connector abstraction actually abstracts, by documenting it and building a trivial second connector (generic syslog) against the guide alone.
acceptance: A guide covers the interface, cursor semantics, normalisation rules and testing requirements
A syslog connector is implemented following only the guide
Building it required no change to ingest, detection or correlation
Any friction encountered is recorded and turned into follow-up tickets

tests.desc: Syslog connector ingests RFC 5424 messages end to end
An engineer unfamiliar with the ingest code builds the connector from the guide alone
